cells.tense: You are reading what's coming in and shifting the blend as it arrives.
cells.ask: Pick one feeling you're already carrying and name what it's asking you to do, then either do that or decide not to — out loud, once.
cells.core:
You adjust as things come in. Someone walks in low and you've already changed how you're standing before you decided to. That isn't a mood you're in; it's a skill, and it's running now.

What keeps it working is that nothing arrives and stays put. You feel it, you shift, you check whether the shift fits, and you shift again. The feeling knows it's a feeling; it doesn't grab the whole table. That's what keeps you close to people without disappearing into them. So the question isn't whether you can receive — it's whether you name what you received. Name one thing that came in today, and what it wanted.
cells.sheetLine: You adjust to what arrives, and it doesn't swallow you.
cells.verb: opening to feel what's arriving before it has a name
cells.place: where you keep adjusting the blend, adding and subtracting as things come in

cells.tense: You are already bracing for how you'll have to adjust to something that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Take one thing you're holding ahead of time — a conversation, a mood you expect, a need you predict — and leave it untouched for a day with no preparing.
cells.core:
You're adjusting to things that haven't shown up. Half your attention is on how someone will feel in three days, what a room might need from you, which version of yourself you'll have to be when it starts. You're not receiving what's here; you're rehearsing what's next.

The rehearsal costs the thing it's for. It's hard to feel what's actually arriving while you're blending for a future that may not ask. When it does arrive, you'll have spent the open part of yourself getting ready for it.

You don't have to stop caring what's coming. Let one of those predicted things sit untouched today — no planning, no pre-shaping yourself around it — and see what the hours feel like when they aren't already narrated.

cells.tense: You used to be open to what was arriving in front of you, and that openness is behind you now.
cells.ask: Sit with one person and one plain piece of what's actually happening for you — no screening first. If nothing can be said, sit with one song and let it land.
cells.core:
The receiving position is behind you. Things come and you answer them from behind glass — you feel the outline of it, not the thing. There's an open making-room that used to happen before you knew what you were making room for, and lately that room isn't opening.

Feeling isn't what's short. The short part is the availability before you've sorted. Pushing feeling into that space doesn't work; it turns into effort and slides off. What works is one thing arriving new — a person, a piece of news, something with no forecast on it — and letting it reach you at the size it actually is.

That readiness is still yours. It just isn't being used on anything current.
cells.sheetLine: You're still receiving, but nothing's getting all the way in.
cells.verb: opening to feel what's arriving before it has a name

cells.tense: You are already calibrating what you give and take by feel, and you talk about it as if it just happens.
cells.ask: Name one exchange from this week — something you gave or received — and say out loud whether it came out even. Don't fix it, just say it.
cells.core:
You keep track of the balance in how you give and take, and you do it well. You notice when you've been absorbing and someone else has been spending, and you adjust — the same adjustment you make to what's arriving, turned toward what's fair.

But you describe it as just how things go, or as the other person's doing, or as nothing. The tuning is yours. It's a skill you're running in the room as you read this, and the one person who gets no credit for it is you.

Naming it is what makes it usable. When the adjustment stays implicit, generosity and habit look the same, and asking for something from a balance you haven't said out loud is hard. Say one of them plainly — to yourself, or to the person it involves.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping the fair balance and calling it nothing.

attempts.check: The record gives the card as 'heart open, ready to receive' and the seat as continuous adjustment, but it never says what the person is open toward or what they are calibrating in a given relationship — the core must stay with the mechanism (adjusting to what's arriving, feeling it early, before it's specific) and let the person name the situation. The strongest unsupported move would be 'you felt something and it didn't land well' in the Too Little cell: the record locates a past anchor but does not say what happened there, so that cell says only that the receiving position is behind the person, not what put it there. The ask survives being wrong in all four cells because each is one small act — naming what a feeling is asking for, deciding one thing and stopping, sitting down with one plain piece of news, naming what one exchange cost — that teaches something about how they hold feeling regardless of whether the diagnosis is exact. The sentence serving the writer more than the person is the one that wants to say 'your heart is open' as praise; cut it, keep the adjustment.
